What can I do with the MCP Security Certification?
AI-powered and agentic systems are now the default infrastructure for modern organizations. This certification gives you practical skills to secure MCP architectures, LLM pipelines, and agentic AI systems. It puts you in position for high-demand roles where traditional security knowledge alone won’t cut it.
Built for People Who Secure AI Systems for a Living
The roles that can’t afford to get this wrong
Senior Security Engineer (MCP Security)
Stop MCP server breaches by enforcing authentication and authorization controls, detecting tool poisoning and prompt injection at runtime, and hardening agentic pipelines before attackers exploit exposed tool interfaces.
AI Security Architect [MCP & Agentic AI]
Eliminate design-level risk in agentic systems by threat modeling MCP architectures with STRIDE and MITRE ATLAS, enforcing zero-trust principles across agent-to-tool communication, and building security into AI infrastructure from the ground up.
Principal Cybersecurity Engineer (MCP Integration)
Prevent supply chain compromise by generating SBOMs, enforcing code signing and provenance attestations, applying SLSA frameworks, and automating security gates across CI/CD pipelines before agentic workloads reach production.
Application Security Lead [Model Context Protocol]
Remove vulnerabilities before deployment by embedding SAST, SCA, and DAST in MCP development pipelines, blocking malicious tool registrations at intake, and securing API surfaces and dependencies across agentic application stacks.

Questions Before You Commit?
Frequently asked questions
What are the prerequisites required before enrolling in the Certified MCP Security Expert Course?
Basic Linux command knowledge is essential before starting this course. While not mandatory, having experience with networking concepts and general security fundamentals will give you an advantage. Familiarity with Python or scripting, AI systems, APIs, or OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities is also beneficial.
What's included in the Certified MCP Security Expert course package?
Your enrollment includes 3-year access to all video content, 60 days of hands-on browser-based labs, a comprehensive PDF manual, 40+ guided exercises, 24/7 support and one certification exam attempt.
Does the Certified MCP Security Expert Course Start Immediately after enrollment?
No, the course doesn’t begin automatically after purchase. Instead, you’ll have the flexibility to choose your preferred start date, and your course access will be activated from your selected date.
E.g., you can start 2 to 3 months later as well.
Does the Certified MCP Security Expert come with CPE points?
Yes, upon completion of the MCP Security Expert course, you’ll earn 36 CPE points.
What is the Exam Format for the Certified MCP Security Expert?
The exam follows a practical format, where you’ll tackle 5 real-world challenges within a 6-hour window. You’ll then have an additional 24 hours to prepare and submit your detailed report for evaluation. For more information, visit this link.
Should I go to an exam center, or is the exam online?
No, it is an online exam. You can take the exam from the comfort of your home or office.
How long is the Certified MCP Security Expert certification valid?
The MCP Security Expert certification is a lifetime credential that never expires. Once you earn it, it remains valid throughout your entire career with no renewal requirements.
How Much More Can You Earn with the Certified MCP Security Expert Course?
The numbers tell the story. Regular Security Engineers make around $110,000, but with CMCPSE certification, you’re looking at $130,000 to $165,000, with top experts pulling in $175,000+. That’s a 15-25% salary increase just for knowing how to secure AI systems and MCP architectures.
Here’s the reality: every company is rushing to adopt AI agents and LLM-powered tools, but almost nobody knows how to secure them properly. It’s still emerging technology, and while everyone is deploying agentic systems left and right, the people who can actually protect these environments are incredibly rare. Without certification, you’re stuck around $80,000 to $100,000 watching others get promoted.
The AI security market is projected to reach $60.6 billion by 2032, and companies are under pressure. They’ve moved quickly to adopt AI but have no idea how to handle tool poisoning, prompt injection, or supply chain risks in agentic systems. When you walk in with CMCPSE certification, you’re not just another security engineer. You’re the person who can actually secure their entire AI stack.
CMCPSE isn’t just a piece of paper either. It’s comprehensive, hands-on training that teaches you real MCP security, not theory, but actual skills you’ll use every day. Security engineers, penetration testers, red teamers, and DevOps professionals are all getting certified because they see what’s coming: if you can’t secure AI systems, you’ll be left behind.
Why choose the Certified MCP Security Expert course from Practical DevSecOps?
Unlike theoretical courses, this vendor-neutral certification provides hands-on experience tackling real-world MCP security challenges. With 24/7 support via Mattermost and browser-based labs, this course will help you become job ready to secure AI and agentic systems for large enterprises.
What you’ll learn:
Attack and defend MCP servers through realistic scenarios and implement proper countermeasures.
Secure agentic AI systems with proper authentication, authorization, and hardening mechanisms.
Apply threat modeling using STRIDE and MITRE ATLAS to identify risks in MCP architectures.
Protect sensitive data with secrets management and detect threats through runtime monitoring and audit logs.
What is the CMCPSE certification?
The Certified MCP Security Expert (CMCPSE) is a first of its kind hands-on certification that teaches security professionals how to identify and fix vulnerabilities in Model Context Protocol (MCP) deployments. It covers the OWASP MCP Top 10, tool poisoning attacks, prompt injection defense, OAuth 2.1 for MCP, and supply chain security for AI agent workflows.
Who should take the CMCPSE course?
Security Engineers, AI Security Architects, Penetration Testers, Red Teamers, DevSecOps Engineers, and AppSec Engineers, MCP Architects working with MCP servers or agentic AI systems should take the CMCPSE course. Developers building production MCP servers will also benefit.
The course fits three kinds of practitioners. Defenders whose organizations are rolling out MCP servers and need to harden them before attackers strike. Offensive security professionals who need to simulate MCP-specific attacks like tool poisoning, prompt injection, and rug-pulls.
Engineers building MCP tools and agentic pipelines who want secure-by-design code from day one. Basic Linux command-line knowledge is required. Familiarity with Python scripting, networking concepts, or the OWASP Top 10 is a plus but not mandatory.
What topics does the CMCPSE cover?
The CMCPSE course covers six areas of MCP security across six chapters:
MCP architecture and the agentic AI ecosystem: hosts, clients, servers, the three primitives (tools, resources, prompts), transport mechanisms (stdio, SSE, HTTP with SSE), and JSON-RPC 2.0.
Attacking MCP servers: tool poisoning, prompt injection via tool responses, rug-pull attacks, cross-server privilege escalation, confused deputy attacks, server impersonation, and resource hijacking.
Threat modeling MCP architectures: STRIDE applied to MCP, data flow diagrams, MITRE ATLAS mapping, OWASP LLM Top 10, risk rating, and IriusRisk-based modeling.
Defending and hardening MCP servers: OAuth 2.0, TLS for SSE/HTTP, RBAC, HashiCorp Vault for secrets, logging, monitoring, and detection.
DevSecOps practices for MCP: SAST, DAST, fuzzing MCP tool inputs, CI/CD security gates, and AI firewalls for runtime protection.
Supply chain security and governance: SBOMs, code signing, SLSA, provenance attestations, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and EU AI Act compliance.
Every chapter ships with hands-on browser-based lab exercises.
What is the CMCPSE exam format?
The CMCPSE exam is a 6-hour practical, hands-on exam with 5 real-world MCP security challenges. After the 6-hour lab window closes, you get an additional 24 hours to compile your findings and submit a detailed report for evaluation.
No multiple-choice. No theory dumps. You either break and fix MCP servers in a live environment, or you don’t pass. The exam is fully online, so you take it from home or the office. No proctor center required.
What is the difference between CMCPSE and CAISP?
CAISP covers broad AI and LLM security: OWASP LLM Top 10, model attacks, AI supply chain risks, MITRE ATLAS, and threat modeling across all LLM deployments. CMCPSE goes deep into one specific layer of the agentic AI stack: the Model Context Protocol and the servers, clients, and tool interfaces that connect LLMs to external capabilities.
Here’s the practical split. CAISP teaches you how to secure AI models and LLM applications. CMCPSE teaches you how to secure the MCP plumbing that lets AI agents take action on external systems. Attacks like tool poisoning, rug-pulls, cross-server privilege escalation, and confused deputy attacks are CMCPSE territory. Prompt injection is covered in both, but CMCPSE specifically handles prompt injection through MCP tool responses.
The two certifications stack well. The CAISP + CMCPSE bundle is priced at $1,529 (regular $1,798), saving $269 for anyone securing production agentic AI systems end to end.
Does the CMCPSE cover the OWASP MCP Top 10?
Yes. CMCPSE covers every attack class currently recognized in the MCP security space, including threats aligned with the OWASP LLM Top 10 and emerging MCP-specific threat taxonomies. Tool poisoning, prompt injection via tool responses, excessive agency, insecure output handling, sensitive information disclosure, and supply chain vulnerabilities all appear in the syllabus with dedicated hands-on exercises.
Chapter 2 works through MCP attack primitives against deliberately vulnerable servers. Chapter 3 maps STRIDE and MITRE ATLAS onto MCP architectures. Chapter 6 handles supply chain risks, including dependency confusion, malicious MCP registries, and agentic worms that propagate autonomously through MCP chains.
